settlements.topic: J2 routes: root paths with ?dept=, and who serves the J2 page
settlements.decision: J2's 28 data routes (23 GET, 5 POST; J2's own index and d3 routes belong to the UI) keep J2's paths at the ROOT of the app and are mounted ONCE. The department is named only by the query parameter ?dept=<department id>, the run only by ?run=<run id> (J2's rule: ?run= is always a read-only disk view). There is no /d/{dept}/api/... copy, no X-Sutra-Dept header and no sutra_dept cookie. A missing or malformed dept gives 400 {'error':'dept_required'}; an unknown department 404 {'error':'not_found'}; a run of another department 404. The J2 PAGE is served only by the UI package: GET / is Home, GET /d/{dept}/ is the J2 page with its boot block, GET /?dept=<id> answers 308 to /d/<id>/. The engine package registers no HTML or static route and has no pages module (its stdlib adapter j2_server.py still serves J2's own page, for the legacy tests only). One constant DEPT_ID_RE = ^[a-z][a-z0-9-]{1,39}$ (ORCH's department-id rule, no underscore) is used by the route dependency, TaskSpec.dept_id and the UI route. The Protocol EngineServices that the routes call is defined only in sutra_app/engine/api/ports.py; ORCH's Services satisfies it.
settlements.why: UI-D2 measured it: J2's page builds root-relative URLs at 28 fetch sites and 15 URL-in-HTML sites, so root paths need ONE fetch wrapper and ONE runQ edit, while a /d/{dept}/api prefix needs 43 edits or a base tag that changes how the 14 href=# anchors resolve. /d/{dept}/ is already the HTML page. J2 assigns location.search on run change and reset (j2_ui.html:3212, 3222), which would drop a ?dept= on the PAGE url, so the department lives in the page PATH and in the API QUERY. One mount means one route table (the engine's double mount registers 56 routes for 28 handlers and doubles the scope tests). ORCH 5.6 and ORCH-D7 as now written already accept ?dept= and ?run=. D6 says the J2 /api/* read endpoints keep their paths so the page works as it did. Checked: no ORCH, LIB or CN route collides with a J2 path (J2 GET /api/runs vs ORCH GET /api/runs/{run_id}; J2 /api/library/{artifact}/{section}/{slug}/v{N} has four segments after /api/library, LIB's /api/library/schemas/{family}/{version} has three); a route-table test keeps it that way.
settlements.rejected: Mounting both (engine 7.2): twice the routes and tests, and the 'delete one line later' decision stays open. Only /d/{dept}/api/... (the ORCH E-1 reading): 43 UI edits or a base tag. An X-Sutra-Dept header or a sutra_dept cookie: invisible state, two tabs on two teams would collide on a cookie. The engine serving the page (engine rows 1-2 and a pages module): the page needs the UI's boot block, CSP and token injection.

settlements.topic: RunSpec.settings and engine flags: who decides what a run gets, and how the owner changes it in Settings
settlements.decision: Three layers, each with one owner and one file. (1) Global defaults: data/engine.json (a partial EngineSettings). (2) Department overrides: data/departments/<dept>/engine.json (partial). (3) Task overrides: RunSpec.settings, a closed set of SEVEN keys (J2_OUTPUT, J2_BUDGET, J2_BUDGET_CAP, J2_FIXES, J2_MEMORY, J2_SLIM, J2_RATES), written by the orchestrator from the start-page output choice (page.json.next_settings, J2_OUTPUT only) and from POST /api/tasks {settings}; TaskService.create validates keys and values (J2_OUTPUT in website|prd|hld|lld; J2_BUDGET and J2_BUDGET_CAP integers 1..100000; the other four '0' or '1') and answers anything else with 422 validation. The ENGINE HOST resolves the effective EngineSettings with EngineSettings.layered(env, global_file, dept_file, task_settings) (order: defaults < data/engine.json < process J2_* env (dev and tests only) < department engine.json < task settings), because only the engine owns the fields and J2's defaults; the orchestrator never reads engine.json. The host writes the effective non-secret values to <run>/settings.json at start; a live run never re-reads files. Every other flag (realization, change, board, template_library, artifact_schema, send_*, chrome, test switches) is reachable only through the two files, never through a task, a model reply or an API field. The owner changes them in Settings through two routes of the engine adapter (api/settings.py, outside J2_PATHS): GET /api/engine/settings[?dept=<id>] returns {schema:'engine-settings/1', defaults, global, department (only with dept), effective, editable:[fields], locked:[fields]}; PUT /api/engine/settings[?dept=<id>] (X-Sutra-Token) takes {set:{field:value}, unset:[field]}, validates with EngineSettings (extra='forbid', secrets are not fields), writes the file atomically (temp file and rename, mode 0600) and answers like GET; unknown, locked or invalid fields give 422 validation. LOCKED_FIELDS (editable only by editing the file by hand): send_mode, send_cap, milestone_emails, test_email, test_slack_target, chrome, force_audit_fail, force_audit_note, force_question, memory_test_lessons. A change applies to the NEXT run of that scope only. The Home Settings pane gets an 'Engine' group (toggles and number fields for the editable fields, locked ones read-only).
settlements.why: J2's defaults stay in one place (EngineSettings) and every J2 flag stays reachable (everything in J2 is present). The seven-key allowlist keeps the dangerous switches (live email, a Chrome path, forced audit failures) out of anything a model reply or a web request can set. The owner needs a way to change flags that is not an environment variable. Only the engine host knows which settings the process really uses, so it must resolve them.
settlements.rejected: Allowing every EngineSettings field in RunSpec.settings; an orchestrator copy of J2's flag defaults (two sources of truth); environment variables only (J2's way, no change from Settings); a SQLite settings table (J2 code and the legacy tests read env and files); letting PUT write the locked fields (a web request could enable live email).

settlements.topic: stop_live: what the orchestrator does and what the engine does on reset
settlements.decision: stop_live(dept_id) -> bool is a plain (sync) method of Services, called only by POST /api/reset?dept=. Semantics: (1) a live task in waiting_user is stopped through the normal stop ladder (S1-contracts-15) and ends 'stopped' with outcome 'reset by you'; (2) the department's queued and blocked tasks are cancelled ('reset by you'); (3) it returns True when no task of the department is starting or running afterwards (including when there was nothing to stop) and False when a task is starting or running, in which case NOTHING is touched; (4) it may block the calling worker thread for at most the stop ladder (12 s) and drives the async stop with anyio.from_thread.run. The engine adapter's reset handler: stop_live False -> 409 {'ok':false} (J2: j2_server.py:264); True -> write page.json.since_run = the department's latest run id (atomic) and answer 200 {'ok':true}. History (tasks, run folders, the department chat in SQLite) is never deleted; the J2 page shows idle until the next task. The engine process does nothing special: it receives the ordinary {'kind':'stop'} inbox line.
settlements.why: Both sections already agreed on the name and the bool. What was missing: the no-task case (J2's 'Try again' button calls reset after a crash, j2_ui.html:1152), queued tasks (a reset page must not start a queued task later), and sync versus async (the engine's routes are plain def run in a thread pool).
settlements.rejected: stop_live killing a running task (J2 refuses; the owner would lose work); reset deleting run folders or chat rows (history); an async stop_live (the engine routes are sync handlers).

settlements.topic: Usage rows: who builds them, who writes the ledger, call_ref, detail, tokens versus usd
settlements.decision: ONE builder, TWO sinks, ONE ledger writer. The connector Router builds exactly one UsageIn per request (success or failure) and hands it to a UsageSink; nothing else builds usage rows. In the server process the sink is UsageStore, which writes usage_ledger directly: that covers the chat agent (AsyncConnector.records_usage = True, so TurnRunner and node panels write no rows of their own) and any server-side call. In an engine process the sink is EventUsageSink (engine/events.py, E0), which appends one 'usage' line to events.jsonl; the server's Projector turns that line into the same ledger row. SQLite is written by the server only (ORCH-D5). The engine host passes the sink to make_port(spec, usage_sink=...) and to ScriptedPort(usage_sink=...), so the helper calls (chat summary, template generator, reviewer, planner, judge) and failed requests are counted too; the plan to emit usage only from call_finished is dropped. UsageIn and UsageSink are defined once, in sutra_app/connectors/usage.py (CN-6), with fields: provider, model, purpose, session_id, node_id, task_id, dept_id, fn, step, atom_id, usd, tokens_in, tokens_out, seconds, ok, how, call_ref, detail; ORCH imports them and keeps only UsageOut. usage_ledger gains step TEXT and atom_id TEXT (no foreign key: a usage line can reach the server before its atom line) with index usage_atom(atom_id); detail_json (nullable) already exists, so connectors agreement A2 on the column is accepted. call_ref = '{run_id}:{call_no}' when tag.call_no > 0 (the id in calls.jsonl), otherwise 'r:{request_id}'; the unique index (task_id, call_ref) with INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING makes any replay harmless. Projector mapping: task_id and dept_id from the task; node_id from fn (function node <dept>.<fn>) or from step (the W-n step node), NULL when that node does not exist yet; session_id from the node; atom_id is stored as given for a function atom and as '<run_id>:<atom id>' for a J2 workflow atom, because J2 atom ids restart at W-1 in every run (S2-models-10). Tokens are the comparable unit and are stored for every provider; usd is stored where the provider reports it (Claude: the list-price estimate, taken as a delta per call) and is NULL for Codex unless the owner filled rates; stub rows are stored with provider 'stub' and excluded from totals (an include_stub=1 query flag shows them); J2 work credits are never converted to usd or tokens. UsageStore.record also calls ChatStore.note_provider so a session's provider chip shows the last provider and model used. CompletionResult.detail carries UsageIn.detail (attempts[{provider, model, effort, code or 'ok', usd, tokens_in, tokens_out, seconds}], cached_in, cache_write, reasoning, usd_basis, billing, cli_version, envelope_id, note, request_id) for callers that want it; ConnectorError.detail carries the same keys for a failed request.
settlements.why: (1) One place builds the row, so attempts, fallbacks, ok=false and detail are right for every caller. (2) The engine's call_finished fires from _log_call, i.e. only for J2Run.call; the other llm.ask sites (j2.py:3113 summary, :8372 template generator, :9514 reviewer, j2_realization.py:685 planner and judge) never reach it, so dozens of calls per realization run would be missing from the ledger. (3) ORCH-D5 stays true. (4) connectors.md 3.8 and engine.md 4.1 already agreed on call_ref; the connectors risk 11 ('ENG and ORCH both say the router writes the ledger') is a misreading and is removed.
settlements.rejected: Usage events built in the llm shim from call_finished (a second builder that misses helper calls and failures); the engine writing SQLite (ORCH-D5); a router without a sink in the engine and the server guessing rows from calls.jsonl; a second UsageIn class in ORCH (two definitions).

settlements.topic: Allowance: how the per-call budget is computed and passed
settlements.decision: Priority's envelope is enforced by the caller that owns it. The engine (J2Run) keeps enforcing money (credits), model_call_limit and retry_limit in its own accounting (j2.py:6896-7120, :7274) and sends allowance=None on every request in v1; the router applies only its own per-request ceiling (max_calls_per_request = 6, policy) and the call timeout. J2 credits are never converted to usd or tokens, so Allowance.max_usd is never derived from an envelope. Allowance stays an optional capability: whoever owns a budget computes it and passes it in CompletionRequest.allowance (engine) or RouteContext.allowance (server); an over-allowance request raises EnvelopeExceededError (kind quota, no fallback) before any process is spawned. The chat agent sends none either (its limits are 3 attempts per stage, 6 requests per owner message, 120 s per call). The function-node layer may later pass Allowance(max_calls=3, envelope_id=<atom id>) per atom; nothing in the wire changes when it does.
settlements.why: Keeps J2's behaviour: J2 counts its own calls against model_call_limit and never counted the llm layer's internal retry; time_limit_minutes and stop_loss are recorded in the envelope but not enforced by J2 code, so enforcing them in the router would change behaviour. Two counters (J2Run and router) would be two truths (connectors CD10 already says so).
settlements.rejected: Passing max_calls = remaining J2 calls (it would forbid the router's one retry and break J2 parity); converting credits to usd; a second independent counter inside the router.

settlements.topic: The final run-event list (the closed RunEvent union on t)
settlements.decision: events.jsonl carries EIGHT event types; every line is one JSON object with t and at (ISO-8601 UTC 'Z', seconds). (1) run.started {pid:int, schema:'events/1', mock:bool, seed:'none'|'rehydrated'|'fresh'}. (2) say {id:int>=1, who:str, text:str, to_user:bool, act:str|null, pause:str|null, questions:list|null, next:str|null}; who is identity|adaptation|priority|coordination|audit|validator|system|W-<n>|team:<role>, never 'user'; this is also how node chat messages travel. (3) node {exactly one of fn:identity|adaptation|priority|coordination|audit or step:W-<n>|team:<role>; status: the nine map/1 words idle|running|waiting|waiting_on_you|fault|filed|done_unchecked|left_open|not_made (a function node uses the first five); detail:str; calls:int; seconds:float; optional task:{id:'t-<turn_no>', kind:str|null, summary:str (<=300), state:'running'|'done', set_by:str}, context:[str] ('<kind>: <summary>', <=200 characters, <=40 items), wait_on:str|null, tokens:{input,output}}; there is NO goal field (a function node's standing goal comes from its FunctionSpec, S2-models-08); a running function node carries task, a waiting one carries wait_on; a function turn starts when task.state is running and ends when it is done; the server derives last_seen from detail while the node is idle and stats from calls, seconds and tokens. (4) step {step:W-<n>|team:<role>, name, parent:str|null, status, handoff:[ref], reads:[ref], rework:ref|null}. (5) atom {node:str, atom:{id, schema:'atom/1'|'work-atom/0.3', goal, work_kind:'llm'|'skill'|'bash'|'manual', verify_template:str|null, status, attempt:0..3, closed_by:'verify'|'manual-override'|null, reason:str|null, body:object, ts_open:int, ts_closed:int|null}} with ts in epoch seconds (library Ts); status is open|closed|verify_failed|abandoned for atom/1 (J2's view) and open|closed|refused|abandoned for work-atom/0.3 (the stored state); for work-atom/0.3 ONLY three more optional fields exist, exactly as S2-models-07 defines them: outcome:'opened'|'verify_failed'|'closed'|'refused'|'abandoned', card:object (library Card) and ledger:object|null (library LedgerRow, null while the atom stays open); updates are forward-only. (6) usage {fn:str, step:str|null, atom:str|null, provider:'claude'|'codex'|'stub', model:str, purpose:str, usd:float|null, tokens_in:int|null, tokens_out:int|null, seconds:float, ok:bool, how:str, call_ref:str, detail:object|null}. (7) heartbeat {} every 5 s. (8) run.ended {status:'done'|'done_with_open_items'|'stopped'|'crashed', outcome:str, code:str|null}, where code is the ModelError code, 'start_failed' or 'internal' for crashed and null otherwise; it is the last line. The session event is REMOVED (J2 calls are one-shot and stateless, so there is no provider session to report; the provider chip comes from usage rows, S1-contracts-05). Producers: run.started and run.ended by the host; say by message_posted; node, step and atom(atom/1) by the StatePublisher (at most every 250 ms, always at turn boundaries, emitted in the order node, step, atom); atom(work-atom/0.3) synchronously by the function-node layer; usage by the Router/ScriptedPort sink; heartbeat by a daemon thread. The host emits run.started AFTER the seed decision (S1-contracts-12); early failures (invalid task.json, failed preflight) emit run.ended only. The Projector applies lines in file order, parses with unknown fields ignored (noted once per run) and unknown types skipped with a note; tests parse strict (extra='forbid'). Projection notes: validator lines go to the session of the function named in next (else Identity's); system lines to Identity's; a speaks_to edge <dept>.<who> -> <dept>.<next> with a message count is projected from every say where both are function names (source {file:'chat.jsonl', field:'next', value:<id>}).
settlements.why: Compared field by field, the engine table (4.5) and ORCH 5.6 agreed on the nine events, but five gaps remained: no timestamp (a replay after downtime would stamp every message with the replay time and reconcile could not judge heartbeat age); the session event fires on every one-shot call (each has a new CLI session id) and carries nothing resumable; usage lacked ok, how, detail and atom; atom status lacked refused (the function-node lifecycle has open, close, refuse, abandon); run.ended lacked a machine-readable code, so the UI could not tell a sign-in problem from a crash.
settlements.rejected: A separate turn event (the node event's task.state already marks start and end and the atom events mark the step; a second source of the same fact); keeping the session event (noise with no resumable id); a seq field (offsets already order the file); a closed-in-production union (a long-lived engine across a server upgrade would lose every event that gained a field).

settlements.topic: What the function-node runtime needs on the wire (turn, atom lines, cost per atom, run end)
settlements.decision: Function nodes add no event type (S2-models-07 agrees). A function turn starts and ends as the node event's task.state running -> done (task id 't-<turn_no>', S2-models-08). Each function turn is one work-atom/0.3 record (S2-models-06). The layer (sutra_app/engine/fnodes/layer.py, selected by SUTRA_HOOKS, S2-models-05) writes every transition as one 'atom' line, synchronously and with the library's outcome, card and ledger row (S2-models-07); the 250 ms publisher writes only atom/1 lines. Every model request of the turn, helper calls included, carries tag.atom = the atom id: the layer binds it with llm.bind_atom(atom_id) right after open_atom and clears it with llm.bind_atom(None) at turn_finished and on every run end path (a process makes one model call at a time, so a module-level binding is safe). The Router builds UsageIn.atom_id from the tag and the usage line carries it as 'atom'; CallInfo.atom reads the same tag. Usage is NOT built from call_finished (S1-contracts-05), so S2-models-07's 'the layer sets CallInfo.atom' is satisfied by the tag. Atom ids and storage keys are S2-models-10's: the library helpers atom_sid and function_atom_id mint function atom ids; J2 workflow atom ids W-n.aK are stored as '<run_id>:<id>' in atoms.id, atom_ledger.atom_id and usage_ledger.atom_id, function atom ids as they are. The Projector fills only what the server knows (session_id, department_id), gates the body, accepts forward moves only, stores the card as a chat message (kind 'card', ChatCard type 'atom') in the node's own session with src_ref '<run_id>#atom:<atom_id>:<outcome>:<attempt>', appends the ledger row when present, and, when a task ends in any way (run.ended, or reconcile marking it crashed or stopped), abandons the task's still-open function atoms with reason 'run ended: <status>' (library abandon_atom). The engine layer abandons its own open atom on the normal and error paths through the existing run_status and run_error hooks; there is no new run_ended hook. A refused open warns and the turn proceeds in v1 (S2-models-06, observe mode).
settlements.why: S2-models-05 to 10 settle the layer's layout, the lifecycle grain, the ids and the atom fields, and S1 must not contradict them; this settlement fixes only the wire points that belong to the process contract. The tag-bound atom id is needed because usage rows are built by the Router (S1-contracts-05), not from call_finished; helper calls (planner, judge, summary) are then charged to the atom that triggered them, as the critics asked.
settlements.rejected: A second event for function atoms; the server minting ids or rendering cards; a new run_ended hook (run_status and run_error already carry the end); usage built from CallInfo.

settlements.decision: D9 is CONFIRMED: every task runs in its own process 'python -m sutra_app.engine --run-dir <dir>', started by the orchestrator in a new session, speaking only through files (task.json and inbox.jsonl in; events.jsonl, snapshot.json, live.json and J2's own files out); the process exits right after it writes run.ended; a run that waits for the owner stays alive; a follow-up is a new process. The ORCHESTRATOR creates the run directory: TaskService.start allocates run_id (j2-YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS-<4 hex>, retried on collision), creates data/departments/<dept>/runs/<run_id>/ with mode 0700 (exist_ok=False), writes task.json atomically (temp file and rename, 0600), creates empty inbox.jsonl and events.jsonl (0600, O_CREAT|O_EXCL), then spawns. The engine NEVER creates its run directory: when --run-dir is missing, is not <data>/departments/<dept>/runs/<run_id>, or task.json fails validation (task.run_id must equal the folder name, task.dept_id the parent folder) the host exits 2, writing run.ended{crashed, code 'start_failed', outcome 'could not start: <reason>'} whenever events.jsonl can be opened and only a stderr line otherwise; J2Run(run_dir=..., run_id=...) never builds a timestamp folder (P3). The engine writes only inside its run folder, plus the department's memory/ folder and the global data/library/ (file-locked, P10). The launcher's child environment is ONE allowlist shared with the connectors: sutra_app.connectors.env.PASS_NAMES (PATH HOME USER LOGNAME LANG LC_ALL LC_CTYPE TMPDIR SSL_CERT_FILE SSL_CERT_DIR the proxy variables and their lower-case twins XDG_CONFIG_HOME XDG_DATA_HOME XDG_CACHE_HOME XDG_STATE_HOME CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR CODEX_HOME) plus SHELL, TERM, PYTHONPATH (worktree runs), every SUTRA_* except SUTRA_TOKEN, and the seven RunSpec.settings keys; never a *_API_KEY, *TOKEN* or *SECRET* name. The connectors' own child env for the CLIs then drops every SUTRA_* again. RunSpec (orchestrator, writer, strict) and TaskSpec (engine, reader, extra='ignore') stay two classes of one document; a contract test proves every RunSpec field exists in TaskSpec and a RunSpec dump validates.
settlements.why: Both sections already say the orchestrator creates the folder (engine F1, orchestrator 5.6) and the engine confirms D9 with measurements (a second run in one process flipped item_kind; module globals NAMES, ROUTES, RATES, OUTPUT, llm.LAST_META). The unnoticed bug: the orchestrator's launcher allowlist (PATH HOME USER LOGNAME SHELL LANG LC_* TERM TMPDIR) is narrower than the connectors' (CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR, CODEX_HOME, XDG_*, proxy and certificate variables); an engine host started without them would hand its CLI children a different login directory and no proxy, so a team could fail to sign in only when run through the app. PYTHONPATH is needed because the repo's scripts/py runs worktrees that way.
settlements.rejected: The engine creating or choosing its folder (race with task.json, needs the data-dir logic twice); threads in the server (shared globals, D9's reason); pipes or RPC to the process (lost on a server restart); two separate allowlists; passing the whole environment (secrets).

settlements.topic: Follow-ups after a run ends: rehydrate versus fresh, and the realization-on pause explained
settlements.decision: A follow-up is always a NEW task: new run id, new folder, new process; the old folder is never written again. seed_from is set (together with parent_run_id) in exactly two places: deliver and deliver_to_department with no live task, which use the department's latest run that has a folder, and TaskService.create(follows=<task of the same department>), which serves the chat agent's AssignmentDraft.follows and POST /api/tasks with a 'follows' field; retry sets parent_run_id only (a retry starts fresh, no files). The engine host decides how to use seed_from: it tries rehydrate(run, src_dir) and falls back to a fresh run with the old files in upstream/<old run id>/ and one plain system line; neither is an error. Rehydrate is allowed when the source summary.json status is done or done_with_open_items, the chat.jsonl header says output website, the source has no document chain (no documents.json, no stage-*.json) and goal.json and workflows.json exist. Realization on or off is NO LONGER a condition. The earlier pause had a cause, found and measured: it is not a rehydrate defect. With J2_REALIZATION on, j2.py:2893 loads NO rate card (load_rates(..., card=False)); the mock Adaptation reply for a change after Done (the feedback branch of mock_plain in _turn_adaptation) gives parts but no estimated_resources, so every workflow costs 0, _register refuses it ('its cost is 0', j2.py:6652) twice, and two empty cycles end in Identity's limit question (j2.py:3465-3469). The same pause happens WITHOUT rehydrate when the same J2Run continues after Done in mock mode; with the rate card put back, the rehydrated run reaches Done (workflows 8 to 9, sites 7 to 8). A real Adaptation fills estimated_resources.money (the format at j2.py:5125 asks for it) and Priority's GRANT carries money_limit, so the real path is expected to work (unverified live). Rehydrate additionally restores real, real_base (a deep copy of goal), real_summary (summary.json realization block minus applied) and real_asked=True when realization.json exists (needed only for J2_CHANGE=1). Refusals stay for: unfinished or stopped or crashed runs, document chains, unreadable files. The system lines are fixed: 'Continuing from run <id>: the team keeps its charter, workflows, findings and site and treats your message as a change request.' / 'Starting a new run. Your earlier files from run <id> are in upstream/<id>/ for reference. Reason: <reason>.' Orphaned question rule: when the owner answers a question whose task has already ended (for example after the app was closed), deliver_to_department creates the follow-up with framing = 'Earlier the team asked the owner: <question text with its options>' and marks that question answered by the new first user line. seed_from must be a run of the SAME department; otherwise it is treated as plain upstream. upstream[].files are paths relative to data/departments/<dept_id>/runs/<run_id>/ of that upstream run; the host resolves them under its data dir, refuses absolute paths, '..' and symlinks that leave the folder, and copies each into upstream/<run_id>/.
settlements.why: J2's change-after-Done flow ('Tell us if you want changes') needs the old state; process-per-run needs a way to bring it back; rehydrate is proven for the classic path and the diagnosis removes the only observed obstacle, while the fresh path keeps every other case working. Probes ran in a scratch copy of J2 ce2631f (rehydrate_probe.py variants under the session scratchpad s1/j2/): realization on, same object, no rehydrate: paused; realization on, rehydrated, rate card restored: Done; with and without restoring real*: Done.
settlements.rejected: Keeping the process alive in standby after Done (81 MB each, breaks the terminal task state); pickling J2Run; refusing follow-ups; a J2 patch P12 that makes the mock reply carry estimated_resources (changes mock prompts and spends the diff budget); always rehydrating regardless of status.

settlements.topic: Non-blocking user_says (P4), the inbox FIFO and stop precedence
settlements.decision: P4 is accepted. J2's user_says takes 'with self.lock' BEFORE it looks at status, and the run thread holds that lock for the whole run, so a call mid-run waits (measured 1.21 s) and then starts a new turn instead of returning False. The vendored method becomes: if not self.lock.acquire(blocking=False): return False (released in finally), plus apply_override(cmd) with the same non-blocking rule. In the app nobody calls user_says from an HTTP thread: the orchestrator answers 409 busy from the task row (starting or running) without asking the engine. The only caller is the host's tick (150 ms), and there the False result is a NORMAL path, not an edge case: the say event of a question is written before the run thread has finished its last steps (summary, report) and set status 'waiting', so an immediate answer must wait. Host rule: inbox lines are read in n order into a FIFO; each tick delivers the head (user -> run.user_says, override -> run.apply_override); False leaves it at the head and writes one trace line inbox.deferred; a stop line is handled the moment it is READ, ahead of the FIFO, and discards everything queued behind it; lines that arrive after run.ended are never read. A user line is delivered only when run.status == 'waiting' (paused or finished-but-not-yet-ended).
settlements.why: It keeps the intent of J2's own check (status == 'running' returns False) which the lock order defeated, and it makes the answer race deterministic instead of lossy.
settlements.rejected: Blocking on the lock in the host (freezes heartbeats and stop handling); dropping a line that finds the run busy (lost answers); letting the orchestrator send lines to a running task (it answers 409 itself).

settlements.topic: SUTRA_MAX_RUNS and the 81 MB idle cost
settlements.decision: Two caps with two reasons. SUTRA_MAX_RUNS (default 3) bounds tasks that are starting or running (CPU and provider-plan concurrency). SUTRA_MAX_LIVE (new, default 12) bounds every live process, including those waiting for the owner (memory: about 81 MB idle each, so about 1 GB at the cap). A run that pauses for the owner (waiting_user) FREES its MAX_RUNS slot, and the Projector calls start_ready() when it does; the owner's answer resumes the same process and is never queued, so MAX_RUNS is a soft limit by at most the number of resumed waiting runs. start_ready starts queued tasks FIFO while running < MAX_RUNS and live < MAX_LIVE; a task that is held back shows the step-node detail 'waiting for a free slot (N teams working)' and GET /api/config exposes both numbers. There is no idle reaper in v1; the owner frees a slot with POST /api/tasks/{id}/stop, and a waiting team is listed with its asked_at in needs-you.
settlements.why: With the cap counting waiting runs, the usual case (the chat agent hands up to five assignments to five teams, and every Identity asks questions at once) would hold three slots idle and starve the other two until a whole run finished. The 81 MB is real (engine.md 2, measured), so memory still needs a bound, but a separate one.
settlements.rejected: Counting waiting runs against MAX_RUNS (starvation); no cap on live processes; a reaper that kills waiting runs after N hours (loses the question context, adds a timer); hibernating a paused run (J2Run cannot be restored from files while paused).

settlements.topic: Graceful server shutdown and the single stop ladder
settlements.decision: One stop ladder for 'stop this task' and for server shutdown, with two constants in orchestrator/runs.py: STOP_GRACE_S = 8 and TERM_GRACE_S = 4. Steps: append {'kind':'stop'} to inbox.jsonl; wait up to STOP_GRACE_S for run.ended (the watcher keeps projecting); then SIGTERM to the process group; wait TERM_GRACE_S; then SIGKILL to the group. Worst case 12 s. At shutdown the ladders of all live tasks (waiting runs included) run in parallel; after each process is gone the watcher drains events.jsonl one last time; the task takes the status of run.ended if one was written, otherwise it becomes stopped with outcome 'the app was closed' (not crashed: the app caused it); then the watchers are cancelled and PRAGMA wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE) runs. The engine's own budget for a stop line is 6 s: port.close() (Router.close kills the CLI children; SIGINT first, so about 1.3 s measured), the host sets stopping so _run_safe's crash path skips the reviewer call and the report, rewrites summary.json to stopped, final publish, run.ended{stopped}, exit 0. SIGTERM does the same without waiting and exits 143. A stopped run is continued by a follow-up (S1-contracts-12): a run stopped while it waited for the owner cannot be rehydrated, so the follow-up is fresh with the old files and the orphaned-question rule.
settlements.why: The three places that gave numbers differed (engine F6 and ORCH 5.1: 5 s then 5 s; ORCH 5.6: 10 s then 5 s). The engine's real work on stop is small (Claude exited in 1.3 s on SIGINT, 2.9 s on SIGTERM), so a single ladder of 8 s and 4 s covers a CLI that ignores SIGINT for its 5 s window and still keeps the app's exit under 12 s.
settlements.rejected: Leaving waiting runs alive when the app closes (invisible idle processes for days, and a stale pid problem); a different ladder for shutdown (two code paths, two tests); SIGKILL first.

settlements.topic: Crash detection by heartbeat and stale-run recovery at server start
settlements.decision: Heartbeat: a daemon thread in the engine writes a heartbeat event every 5 s (SUTRA_HEARTBEAT_S overrides, tests use 0.2), starting after run.started, even while the run thread is blocked in a model call; it proves the PROCESS lives, not that the run progresses. Every event carries at, and tasks.last_event_at is the 'at' of the newest applied line (event time, not receipt time). Rule while the server runs: a task is crashed when no terminal event exists and launcher.alive(pid) is False after one final drain (outcome 'the team process stopped unexpectedly', exit code when known, redacted stderr tail up to 2 KB); a silent but alive process is NOT killed (a sleeping laptop freezes both sides); the step node detail shows 'no signal for N s' after 30 s. Rule at server start, reconcile(), for each task in starting, running, waiting_user: (1) drain events.jsonl from events_offset, applying complete lines in batches (the heartbeats written while the server was down refresh last_event_at); (2) a terminal event settles the task through the normal projection; (3) else, pid alive and now - last_event_at <= 30 s: re-attach the watcher from events_offset; (4) else, pid alive but silent over 30 s: only if 'ps -p <pid> -o command=' contains 'sutra_app.engine --run-dir <that dir>' run the stop ladder, otherwise signal nothing (pid reuse); then crashed ('the app was closed while it ran and the team stopped answering'); (5) pid gone: crashed ('the app was closed while it ran'); (6) starting with no pid: crashed ('could not start'); starting with a live pid and no event within 30 s of the spawn (last_event_at is seeded with the spawn time): the same as rule (4). Every crashed task also abandons its open work atoms (S1-contracts-10). reconcile runs after migrate and bootstrap and before start_ready(); it ends by publishing server.resync {reason:'restart'}.
settlements.why: Orchestrator 5.1 gave the rule only in outline (pid gone or heartbeat older than 30 s) and judged age from receipt time, which is wrong after downtime; with 'at' on every line the age is the engine's own. The identity check avoids killing an unrelated process that reused the pid.
settlements.rejected: Killing silent-but-alive processes while the server runs (false positives on sleep, long model calls still beat); judging staleness by the time the server reads the line; trusting the pid alone.

settlements.topic: Owner override key and the .env file: the server holds the key, the engine only sees the command
settlements.decision: The SERVER owns J2_OVERRIDE_KEY. Settings gets override_key (secret: never serialised, never in /api/config, logs, events or stored text), read from the process environment or from the .env file named by SUTRA_ENV_FILE (default <project>/.env). deliver() and deliver_to_department() strip the text; if it starts with the key (hmac.compare_digest on the prefix, as J2 matches the start, j2.py:3368) the line is an OVERRIDE: it is accepted only for a live task in waiting_user (otherwise 409 busy, a system note 'Owner override needs a team that is waiting for you.' in the department session, and NO task is ever created from it); the inbox receives {n, kind:'override', cmd:<text after the key>, at}; the department session stores only 'Owner override sent'. The engine host never sees the key: its child environment has no J2_OVERRIDE_KEY, load_env_file loads only J2_SMTP_* into the engine, and apply_override (P4) runs the command; J2's own system line ('Owner override applied: ...') comes back as a say event. redact (ORCH-1) builds its secret set exactly like j2_server.py:29-43: every value of an environment variable whose name contains KEY, TOKEN, SECRET, PASSWORD or AUTH, plus every value in the .env file, minimum length 8, longest first; it is applied to every API body, SSE payload, log line, stored chat text and stderr tail.
settlements.why: Engine 4.4 says 'the server checks the key' and ORCH 5.5 says the same, but ORCH's Settings (closed, extra forbid) has no field for the key and no section loads .env, so J2's owner override (budget +N, ship, drop) could not work and redaction could not find the .env secrets. SUTRA_ENV_FILE is already in the engine's variable list but missing from ORCH's env table.
settlements.rejected: The engine checking the key (it would need the secret in a child process); storing the key in SQLite or under data/; matching the key anywhere in the text (J2 matches the start); creating a follow-up task from an override line that has no waiting team.
